## What it is

Advanced Data Engineering, Summer 2026. The brief was to stand up a real
warehouse over Prague metro tap records and then answer operational questions
with it: who rides, when, from where, and for how long. Roughly 443,000 rides
across four fare types (standard, student, senior, and weekly passes), joined to
station, zone, and time dimensions.

The point of the course was the plumbing, but the deliverable that gets judged is
whether anyone can act on what comes out the other end.

## What I built

**Warehouse.** A PostgreSQL warehouse on a shared Linux VM, containerized with
Docker Compose and persistent storage, modeled as a star schema with fact and
dimension tables.

**Pipeline.** Airflow DAGs that snapshot source data into an S3-compatible data
lake as Parquet, then load it into warehouse staging tables. Getting every table
to load reliably meant working through file-read and database-connection failures
rather than rerunning by hand.

**Transformations.** dbt models that turn staging into dimension tables with
reproducible, re-runnable loads, using hashed surrogate keys so joins stay stable
when the source refreshes.

**Dashboards.** Grafana, built as two panels of analysis rather than a wall of
charts, with written interpretation sitting next to each figure instead of buried
in a legend.

## What the dashboards show

![Ride duration analysis: overall average, breakdown by hour, zone, fare type, and day of week, with an entry-station map.](milestone3-dashboard.png){fig-alt="Grafana dashboard showing a 37 minute average ride duration, bar charts by hour of day and zone, a fare type table, and a geographic map of Prague stations colored by average ride duration" width="100%"}

**Ride duration is remarkably flat, except where geography explains it.** The
system-wide average is 37 minutes. Day of week barely moves it, which means heavy
weekday volume is not translating into longer trips. What does move it is
distance from the center: stations on the outer edges of the network, like
Letňany and Černý Most, average an hour or more, and Zone 2 departures run the
longest of any zone while Zone 1 runs the shortest.

**Weekly pass holders behave like a different population.** They average 27.8
minutes against roughly 39 for standard fares, they cluster tightly in the
historic center around Můstek and Staroměstská, and about 45% of their taps land
at only five stations. They also peak Sunday and Monday while every other fare
type peaks midweek. Tourists, in other words, and the data says so without anyone
having to assert it.

**Students shift the rush hour an hour earlier.** Student taps peak at 07:00 and
16:00; standard fares peak at 09:00 and 17:00. That is a schedule-planning fact,
not a curiosity.

![Fare group usage patterns: station clustering map, concentration by fare group, ridership by day of week, and hourly ridership by fare type.](milestone2-dashboard.png){fig-alt="Grafana dashboard showing a map of student rider tap locations across Prague, a bar chart of usage concentration by fare group, ridership by day of week, and hourly tap counts by fare type" width="100%"}

## What I would do differently

The map was the strongest panel and also the least explained. Dot size encodes
ride volume and nothing on the dashboard says so, which means the most
information-dense figure depends on the viewer guessing the encoding. I would
also lay the panels out to follow how people actually read, top to bottom and
left to right, so the argument builds in order rather than requiring the viewer
to hunt for it.

The concentration finding (weekly riders clustering at five stations) was real
analysis buried in a chart that did not make it obvious, and the fact that one
panel showed only the five busiest stations was disclosed in a description rather
than in the title. Both are labeling problems, not analysis problems, which is
exactly the kind of thing that separates a chart that works from one that needs a
caption to rescue it.
